Storm season readiness checklist for roofing companies

Storms create demand overnight. This checklist covers what needs to be ready before the next one, so that demand turns into inspections and signed roofs.

Published July 8, 2026 · 4 min read

Why prepare now

When a storm hits, search demand for roof inspections and repairs can jump overnight. The companies that win are the ones ready to answer, book and inspect quickly, with campaigns that switch on in hours rather than days. Everything on this list is easier to do in a quiet month.

Use this as a working list. Assign each item an owner and a date, and revisit it at the start of every season. Some items take an afternoon; others, like inspection capacity, need real planning with the operations team.

Website and landing pages

  • A storm-damage page that explains the inspection process in plain language.
  • Online inspection booking that works well on a phone.
  • Clear proof: licences, insurance, warranties, reviews and local project photos.
  • Guidance on what homeowners should document for insurance.

Campaigns ready to switch on

  • Paid search campaigns built and paused, with storm-specific ad copy.
  • Service-area targeting that can be narrowed to affected neighbourhoods.
  • Email and text templates for past customers in the affected area.
  • A daily budget ceiling agreed in advance.

“A storm is not the time to write ad copy.”

Phones and scheduling

  • Overflow routing or answering service for the first days after a storm.
  • A short script that books an inspection on the first call.
  • Inspection slots held back for storm demand.
  • Text confirmations and reminders to cut no-shows.

In practice · Roofing

Inspection crews pre-assigned by zone, with booking slots released in the first 48 hours after a storm instead of first-come, first-served.

Trust and reputation

After storms, homeowners are wary of out-of-town crews. Make it easy to see that you are local, established and accountable: a physical address, local reviews, and named team members.

Tracking and follow-up

What to track for every storm
MetricWhy
Inspection requests by sourceShows which campaigns to turn on first next time
Time from request to inspectionUsually the biggest driver of signed jobs
Inspection-to-contract rateMeasures sales and trust, not just demand
Claims in progressKeeps long insurance cycles from falling through the cracks

After the storm: follow through

Storm work has a long tail. Insurance claims take weeks, homeowners get second opinions, and some decide to wait until spring. The companies that win more of that work keep in touch in a helpful, unhurried way: an update on the claim process, a reminder about documentation, a check-in when the adjuster visit is due.

Keep a separate pipeline view for storm inspections so they don’t get mixed with routine leads. Each inspection should have an owner, a next step and a date. When the next storm comes, last season’s data on which campaigns and neighbourhoods produced signed roofs will tell you where to focus first.

Finally, ask for reviews once the work is done. A homeowner who just went through an insurance claim with your help is often glad to say so, and those reviews are exactly what the next wary storm customer wants to read.

The short version

  1. Build and pause storm campaigns now.
  2. Publish a storm-damage page with clear booking.
  3. Agree overflow call cover and inspection capacity.
  4. Tag storm leads so you can learn from them.

Key takeaways

  • Prepare pages, campaigns and scripts before the season, not after the storm.
  • Speed of inspection booking matters more than ad volume.
  • Trust signals carry extra weight after storms.
  • Track storm leads separately to learn for next year.
